contributions.headingText: Lymphomatoid papulosis (LyP) belongs to the spectrum of primary cutaneous CD30-positive T-cell lymphoproliferative disorders. It is characterized by self-healing but recurrent papulonodular skin lesions, atypical CD30-positive T cells by histology, and an excellent prognosis.

9718/1 Primary mucosal CD30-positive T-cell lymphoproliferative disorder

9718/1 Lymphomatoid papulosis subtypes A, B, C, D, E

9718/1 Lymphomatoid papulosis with DUSP22 locus rearrangement
Primary mucosal CD30-positive T-cell lymphoproliferative disorder; lymphomatoid papulosis subtypes A, B, C, D, and E; lymphomatoid papulosis with DUSP22 locus rearrangement

LyP most frequently involves the trunk and extremities {10845893}. The disease may have primary mucosal involvement or, rarely, can concurrently involve various mucosal and cutaneous sites {15604547; 22388754}.

LyP manifests with recurrent eruptions with a waxing and waning course of papulonodular skin lesions that may ulcerate {5634442}. The number of lesions may vary from a few to more than a hundred. Occasionally, larger (up to 20 mm) and longer-persisting nodular lesions can develop. Characteristically, skin lesions in different stages of evolution coexist {10845893; 21982062}. The individual skin lesions spontaneously regress within 3–12 weeks, leaving scars and/or hypopigmentation or hyperpigmentation {5634442}. LyP may persist for several months, or occasionally for years or decades {14639383; 21982062}.

The incidence is 1.2–1.9 cases per 1 million person-years, and the M:F ratio is 2–3:1 {14710887; 10845893; 21982062; 14639383}. LyP most often affects adults (median age at onset: 35–45 years), but children may also be affected {11251571; 19577330; 32172217; 27138554}.

The cause of LyP is largely unknown. Atopy and staphylococcal superantigens have been pathogenetically linked to LyP {32049976}. A viral etiology has been suggested, but not proved {8227605; 8393923; 11168749}. Endogenous retroviral elements (i.e. inherited genomic elements with structural features of integrated retroviruses) have been detected, but their etiological role is unclear {12584181; 31883959}.

The translocation t(2;5)(p23;q35), resulting in ALK expression, is not detected in LyP {8605362}. Identical T-cell clones have been demonstrated in some LyP lesions and associated lymphomas {8618007; 25666664; 1532439}. Rearrangements of the DUSP22 locus on chromosome 6p25.3 are found in a small subset of LyP cases {23648461; 21169992}. NPM1::TYK2 translocation, STAT mutations, and oncogenic fusion transcripts activating the JAK/STAT pathway have been identified {25349176; 32147503}. SATB1 is expressed in the vast majority of LyP cases {29510190}.
The lesions present as papules and small nodules (see Clinical features).

The histological spectrum of LyP is extremely broad and in part depends on the evolution of the biopsied lesion {7104214; 14710887; 15096372; 15096372; 29719017}. Six main subtypes (A–E and with 6p25.3 rearrangements involving the DUSP22 locus) with distinct histological and/or genetic features are delineated (see #29769Table 5.10) {7104214; 10845893; 15096372; 20661014; 23026936; 23648461}. They may occur in different but concurrent lesions, and a single LyP lesion may show overlapping histological features of the different subtypes of LyP {15096372; 14710887; 29719017}. Other rare subtypes have been described, including folliculotropic, syringotropic, and granulomatous LyP {23375516; 23348211; 12760293}. Mucosal lesions show a similar spectrum of findings {15604547; 22388754}.

Immunohistochemistry

The atypical lymphoid cells express CD30, often with a Golgi dot-like pattern. They predominantly express CD4 in LyP subtypes A, B, and C; express CD8 in LyP subtypes D and E; and either express CD8 or are double-negative for CD4/CD8 in LyP with DUSP22 locus rearrangement. Atypical cells may express TIA1 {9347791}. Rare cases expressing CD56, TCRγδ, or a T follicular helper (TFH) cell phenotype have been reported {32568843; 11531801; 17052504}.

Differential diagnosis

Although the LyP subtypes do not have any prognostic or therapeutic implications, recognition of these subtypes is important to avoid misdiagnosis of other, more aggressive lymphomas. Clinicopathological correlation is essential for differentiating LyP not only from these lymphomas but also from a wide variety of infectious and inflammatory skin diseases that can contain a substantial number of CD30+ cells {20043512; 16412214; 18616762}.
Fine core needle biopsy is not recommended for making this diagnosis.
Monoclonal rearrangements of TR (TCR) genes can be detected in 22–80% of LyP cases {8618007; 8288780; 12091351; 17083688}.

Essential: infiltrates of mostly medium-sized atypical lymphoid cells with expression of CD30 and T-cell markers, and a variable inflammatory background; clinical presentation with waxing and waning papulonodular skin lesions; spontaneous regression within weeks to a few months; exclusion of other lymphomas by clinicopathological correlation.

Desirable: detection of monoclonal rearrangement of TR genes may be helpful in selected cases (especially in LyP subtype A).
In patients with the typical clinical presentation and no indication of extracutaneous disease by physical examination or blood tests, there is no need for further staging {21841159; 20026848}.

LyP has an excellent prognosis. However, patients are at increased risk for being diagnosed with a secondary cutaneous lymphoma (mycosis fungoides, primary cutaneous anaplastic large cell lymphoma), which may precede, be associated with, or follow LyP {26518172; 10845893; 21982062; 10506709; 26668250; 14639383; 1532439; 28614957; 31715046}. An increased risk for various non-haematological malignancies, such as cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma, melanoma, and organ-based malignancies, has also been suggested {31715046; 10506709}. Demonstration of fascin expression by CD30-positive cells and clonal TR gene rearrangement in LyP were suggested as risk factors for the development of LyP-associated lymphomas, pending confirmation in larger studies {21982062; 12100631}. Because of the increased risk of associated lymphomas, long-term follow-up is advised {21841159; 14710887}.
